summary: A report from the IAB and GSMA workshop on managing radio networks in an encrypted world, held in September 2015. It discusses how mobile network bandwidth optimization, which relied on seeing unencrypted content, can work as traffic becomes encrypted.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone networks used to peek at traffic to speed it up. Now traffic is sealed, so experts met to talk about how to help without peeking.

questions: how do mobile networks optimize encrypted traffic
bandwidth optimization without deep packet inspection
subtitle: How radio networks can optimize traffic as encryption becomes the norm.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks have long optimized bandwidth by inspecting unencrypted traffic to prioritize interactive content over background data and cache frequently accessed material. As encryption becomes standard, these techniques no longer work, potentially harming performance on radio networks with limited spectrum.
tldr.mechanism: The MaRNEW workshop brought together IETF engineers, mobile operators, and content providers to identify solutions. The group discussed metadata sharing between endpoints and networks, transport-layer improvements, new caching strategies for encrypted content, and cooperative approaches where networks and applications share information without breaking encryption.
tldr.outcome: The workshop produced principles and solutions including evolving TCP, improving CDN caching near users, explicit API-based capacity sharing, congestion control improvements, and stronger collaboration between standards bodies. Many proposals were later discussed in IETF working groups, with some leading to new protocols like QUIC.

facts.label: Participants
facts.value: Over 50 from operators, CDNs, manufacturers, IETF

today: RFC 8462 is an Informational report published in October 2018. It documents outcomes of the 2015 MaRNEW workshop. The report has not been obsoleted. Since its publication, QUIC has been standardized (RFC 9000), congestion control research has advanced, and conversation between IETF and mobile operators has deepened, confirming the workshop's value.

sections.title: The Problem and the Workshop
sections.content: In September 2015, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the GSM Association (GSMA) jointly hosted a two-day workshop called MaRNEW—Managing Radio Networks in an Encrypted World. At that time, roughly 50 percent of internet traffic was encrypted and rising. Mobile networks have unique constraints: the radio spectrum is shared, bandwidth is expensive, and the network is heavily engineered to prioritize critical traffic (emergency services, interactive voice) over bulk data. For decades, optimization relied on middle boxes (network appliances) that inspected unencrypted traffic to identify and prioritize application types. Increasing encryption threatened this model. The workshop aimed to explore how mobile networks could continue optimizing traffic without breaking encryption or violating user privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: Two big groups met to figure out how phone networks can stay fast when nobody can peek at the data passing through.

sections.title: What Is Bandwidth Optimization?
sections.content: For the workshop, bandwidth optimization includes caching (storing copies of popular content closer to users), traffic prioritization (giving emergency and interactive traffic preference over bulk downloads), per-user bandwidth caps, and policy-based filtering (parental controls, legal interception where required by law). Some of these functions—like caching—can continue largely unchanged with encryption. Others, like identifying a video stream to prioritize it, depend on seeing unencrypted traffic. The workshop scoped the discussion to assume unbreakable encryption, no lawful interception by breaking encryption, and a goal of improving user experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Bandwidth optimization means making networks faster by knowing what kind of data is being sent, like knowing to slow down a big download when a phone call arrives.

sections.title: Solutions Proposed: Sharing Data Without Peeking
sections.content: Most solutions discussed at MaRNEW centered on metadata exchange: sharing information about traffic without opening the encrypted package. Mobile Throughput Guidance (MTG) allows a network to tell a TCP sender how much bandwidth is available right now. The Network Status API lets an app ask the network about congestion before it starts sending. Congestion Exposure (ConEx) lets packets announce how much congestion they experienced, helping the network understand bottlenecks. Session Protocol for User Datagrams (SPUD) and later protocols like QUIC separate protocol negotiation from data encryption, allowing middleboxes to see enough about the traffic to help coordinate, while the payload stays sealed. Others proposed letting applications explicitly declare whether they need high bandwidth or low latency, and fixing lower-layer protocols (like TCP) to handle radio networks better.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of peeking at your data, the network and your app exchange hints: "I have 5 Mbps available," "I need low delay," "I am a video call," and so on.

sections.title: Privacy and Trust
sections.content: The workshop emphasized that user privacy must come first. Any solution that gathers data about a user or their traffic is sensitive and must be opt-in. Many participants agreed that if middleboxes are involved, they should be explicitly invoked rather than transparent. Content providers worried about revealing traffic patterns and worried that they bear the cost if networks fail to deliver quality. Network operators worried about competitive data leaking to rivals. The workshop noted that regulations differ by region: some require lawful intercept capabilities, others mandate data protection. The group concluded that encryption should not be weakened, and that solutions should be switched off easily if they cause problems.
sections.plainLanguage: If the network collects data about what you do, you should know about it and be able to say no.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions and Progress Since the Workshop
sections.content: The workshop identified several families of solutions: transport-layer evolution (improving TCP or adopting new protocols like QUIC), application-layer optimization (caching encrypted content with Keyless SSL and Blind Caching, placing CDN caches closer to users), cooperative traffic management (bidirectional data exchange between network and apps), and better queue management and congestion control. Since 2015, many of these ideas advanced. QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) emerged as a practical protocol that solves transport problems independent of TCP. Work on caching encrypted content continued in the IETF HTTPbis working group, though proposals had security flaws that required rework. Some proposed mechanisms like PLUS (Path Layer UDP Substrate) and LURK (Limited Use of Remote Keys) generated more questions than solutions and did not result in new working groups. The most enduring outcome was increased collaboration: mobile operators and IETF engineers established relationships and continue working together on shared standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ideas became real (QUIC, better congestion control), some are still being worked on (caching), and some turned out to be harder than expected. But the networks and the internet community started talking to each other, and that was a win.
